title: What Does the Lord's Supper Actually Mean?
subtitle: Jesus left his church not a theory but a meal. Bread broken, a cup poured, a command to keep eating until he comes. What Scripture, the ancient church, and the range of faithful Christian views say about the meaning of communion, the gospel you can taste, the presence of Christ at the table, and the meal that has been forming a people for two thousand years.

connections.label: Consumer Faith and the Communal Church

parts.title: The Meal You Eat Without Knowing What It Is
parts.body:
Once a month, or once a week, the tray comes down the row, and you take the small piece of bread and the little cup, and you bow your head, and you are not entirely sure what just happened. You were told to examine yourself, so you ran a quick inventory of the week's sins and felt vaguely guilty. You were told it was important, so you treated it with a solemnity you could not quite explain. And then it was over, and you went back to your seat, and a part of you wondered, in a place you would not say out loud, whether any of it was real or whether you were chewing a cracker and remembering a man who died a long way away.

You are not faithless for wondering. You have simply never been taught what you are holding. Somewhere along the way the meal that the early Christians risked their lives to eat became, for many of us, a tacked-on appendix to the sermon, a quiet five minutes of private reflection, a personal moment of being sorry for our sins squeezed in before the closing song. We made it small. We made it individual. We made it a feeling we generate inside our own heads. And then we wondered why it felt thin.

Meanwhile the questions sit underneath, unanswered. Is Christ actually present in this, or only in my memory of him. Why bread and wine, why these particular things, why a meal at all. Why did Jesus, on the last night of his life, with everything he could have left us, leave us this. And why has the church, in every century and on every continent, gathered to do this one strange thing, in catacombs and cathedrals, in prison cells and prairie churches, as though their lives depended on a bite of bread and a swallow from a cup.

Let me say it plainly. The Lord's Supper is not a footnote to the gospel. It is the gospel made edible, the only thing Jesus ever told us to keep doing in remembrance of him, a meal he chose over a creed because he wanted his death lodged not just in our minds but in our mouths, our bodies, our shared table, week after week, until the world is made new. You have been eating the center of the faith and treating it like a garnish. It is time to learn what is on the plate.

parts.title: What We Lose When the Table Goes Small
parts.body:
The stakes begin with a quiet theft we did not notice happening. The modern church reduced the Supper to a private moment of personal piety, a time to feel sorry and feel grateful inside your own skull, and in doing so it stripped the meal of nearly everything Scripture says it is. We turned a feast into an introspection. We turned a family meal into a row of strangers each alone with their thoughts. And a gospel that was meant to be tasted, shared, and embodied became, like so much of our faith, an idea managed privately in the head. The thinning of the table is a symptom of the thinning of the whole Christian life, and we did it to ourselves.

The stakes are pastoral, because we are forming people who do not know how to receive grace they cannot earn. The Supper is the one moment in the Christian week where you do nothing but receive. You do not perform. You do not contribute. You hold out empty hands and are given the body and blood of Christ, broken and poured for you while you were still a sinner. A church that loses the table loses its most regular, bodily lesson in grace, and it raises Christians who intellectually believe in grace and emotionally still believe they must earn their place. The table preaches with bread what the sermon can only describe with words, that you are fed before you are fixed.

The stakes are communal, and this is where the watching skeptic sees what we have become. The Supper was meant to make many into one. Paul says it bluntly, that because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one loaf. The meal was a weekly enactment of the impossible, slave and master, Jew and Gentile, rich and poor eating from one loaf as one family, and that visible oneness was an argument the ancient world could not answer. We have turned it into individuals sipping from sealed plastic cups, sealed off from one another even in the act that was supposed to bind us, and the unbelieving neighbor sees, correctly, a religion of private consumers and not a new humanity.

And the stakes are eternal, because the table is the rehearsal of the end. Every time the church eats this meal, Paul says, it proclaims the Lord's death until he comes, holding the cross and the second coming together in one bite. The Supper is a clock and a compass. It points back to a real death on a real Friday and forward to a real feast at the end of all things, and it locates you, right now, as a person living between the cross and the consummation, fed on the way. Lose the table and you lose the most concrete thing the church does to remember where the story has been and where it is going. A people who forget how to eat this meal will, soon enough, forget the death and the coming it was given to keep alive.

parts.title: Bread, Cup, and the Whole Story of God
parts.body:
Go back to the night it began, because everything starts there. It is the night before the cross, and Jesus is keeping the Passover, the oldest meal of his people, the feast that remembered the night God passed over Israel and brought them out of slavery through the blood of a lamb. For fifteen centuries Israel had eaten that meal and told that story. And now Jesus takes the bread of that ancient feast and does something staggering. He breaks it and says, this is my body, given for you. He takes the cup and says, this is my blood of the covenant, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. He is standing inside the Passover and announcing that he is the Lamb, that the exodus the whole meal pointed to is about to happen on a cross, and that the deliverance from a deeper slavery is about to be bought with his own blood.

That is the first thing the Supper is. It is the new Passover, the new exodus, the deliverance of God reaching its climax. When you take the bread and the cup you are not remembering a sad death in isolation. You are being placed inside the longest story in the world, the story of a God who keeps coming down to set his people free, from Egypt, from Babylon, and finally from sin and death itself, and who has now done it for you in the body and blood of his Son. The meal carries the whole arc, all the way back to a doorpost painted with blood so the angel of death would pass over a household, all the way forward to a cross where the firstborn Son was not spared so that you would be.

The second thing the Supper is, it is communion, real participation, not bare memory. Paul asks the Corinthians a question that assumes a yes, the cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ, the bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ. The word he uses is koinonia, sharing, fellowship, a genuine joining. Whatever else faithful Christians have disagreed about, and they have disagreed, the New Testament will not let the Supper shrink into a mere mental exercise. Something is given here. Christ is encountered here. The believer who eats in faith is joined to the crucified and risen Lord and to all his people, and that joining is the whole point of the word communion.

The third thing the Supper is, it is the meal of a body that must be one. The longest passage on the Supper in the New Testament is not abstract theology. It is Paul furious at a church for eating it wrongly. In Corinth the rich were feasting while the poor went hungry at the same table, and Paul says that when you do that, it is not the Lord's Supper that you eat, that you are eating and drinking judgment on yourselves because you do not discern the body. He means the church. To eat the bread that makes many one while despising your brother is to eat a lie, and to examine yourself before the table is first of all to ask whether you are at peace with the people you are about to eat beside. The table that does not make you one with your neighbor has not been rightly eaten.

The fourth thing the Supper is, it is a foretaste, a down payment on a feast that has not yet come. Jesus said at that last supper that he would not drink again of the fruit of the vine until he drank it new with them in his Father's kingdom. The meal leans forward. It is hungry. It is the appetizer of the marriage supper of the Lamb, the great feast at the end of Revelation where the redeemed of every nation finally sit down together with their God and the long ache of the world is healed in a banquet. Every communion is a rehearsal of that day, a small and stubborn taste of the kingdom that is coming, eaten by a people who are still hungry and now know exactly what they are hungry for.

And hold all four together and you see why Jesus left us a meal and not a memo. He could have left us a doctrine to recite. Instead he left us bread to break and a cup to share, because the gospel is not finally a concept to be grasped but a gift to be received, and the surest way to keep a truth from drifting into the abstract is to make a people eat it. The Word became flesh, and the Word gives himself to us in things we can taste. That is not a concession to the simple. It is the very logic of the incarnation. The God who took on a body feeds his people with bread, and a faith that grows embarrassed by the physical has grown embarrassed by the manger and the cross.

parts.title: The Meal the Church Could Not Stop Eating
parts.body:
From the first generation, the church organized its life around this meal. The Didache, a manual of Christian practice from perhaps the late first century, already gives prayers for the bread and the cup, thanking God for the life and knowledge made known through Jesus, and pictures the scattered grain gathered into one loaf as a prayer that the scattered church might be gathered into the kingdom. The meal was there from the beginning, with thanksgiving at its heart, which is why the church came to call it Eucharist, the Greek word for thanksgiving. Before there was a New Testament bound in one volume, there was a people breaking bread.

By the middle of the second century we have a remarkably full description. Justin Martyr, writing around the year 150 to explain Christian worship to a hostile empire, describes how the believers gather on the day called Sunday, hear the memoirs of the apostles read aloud, pray, and then bring bread and wine, give thanks over them at length, and share them, with portions carried by the deacons to those who are absent. Justin says plainly that the church did not receive these as common bread and common drink, and he ties the meal to the incarnation, that as Jesus took flesh and blood for our salvation, so this food is the flesh and blood of that same Jesus. Whatever later refinements came, the early church already held that something real was given here.

Augustine, in the late fourth and early fifth centuries, gave the Western church language it has never let go of. He called the sacrament a visible word, a sign that does what the preached word does but through the eyes and the mouth. And he turned the meal back on the people who ate it, telling his congregation in a famous Easter sermon that they themselves were on the table, that they were the body of Christ they received, and that they should become what they received. For Augustine the Supper was never magic and never bare memory. It was a sign that united the believer to Christ by faith and bound the church together as one loaf, one body, given to one another as much as to God.

The medieval church, working with Aristotle through Thomas Aquinas in the thirteenth century, developed a careful philosophical account of how the presence could be real, the doctrine that came to be called transubstantiation, that the substance of the bread and wine became the body and blood of Christ while the outward appearances remained. Aquinas wrote some of the most beautiful eucharistic hymns the church possesses, adoring a Lord he believed was truly present, hidden under the form of bread. We do not have to share his philosophy to feel the weight of his reverence, a man kneeling before a wafer because he was convinced his Savior was there.

Then came the sixteenth century, and the Reformation broke partly over this table. Martin Luther, beginning in 1517, threw off much of the medieval apparatus but held fiercely to the real presence, insisting that when Christ said this is my body, he meant it, and famously chalking those four words on the table at the Marburg meeting in 1529 and refusing to wipe them away. Ulrich Zwingli in Zurich took the other road, reading this is my body as this signifies my body, and emphasizing the Supper as a memorial, a solemn act of remembrance and pledged loyalty by a grateful people. John Calvin in Geneva charted a path between them, teaching that Christ is truly given to the believer in the Supper, not by the bread becoming his body but by the Holy Spirit lifting the believer up to feed on the living Christ in heaven, a true spiritual presence received by faith. Against all of this the Roman Catholic Church at the Council of Trent, meeting across the middle of the century, reaffirmed transubstantiation and the sacrifice of the Mass, and the lines were drawn that still mark the churches today.

It is worth feeling the gravity of that history before we rush past it. Christians did not divide over the Supper because they thought it unimportant. They divided over it because every one of them thought it was the holiest thing the church does and could not bear to get it wrong. Men went to the stake over how to read four words at a table. That should chasten anyone who finds the meal boring. The whole church, across every century and every painful division, has agreed on the one thing that matters most, that Jesus told us to keep eating this until he comes, and that in it, somehow, we meet him. The disagreements are real and we will weigh them honestly. But they are family arguments about how a treasure works, conducted by people who all knew it was a treasure.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: Human beings have always known, beneath their theories, that shared meals and physical rituals do something to us that words alone cannot, and honest observers from anthropology to psychology have studied why. A believer can receive what they have learned gratefully and critically at once, because all truth is God's truth. What follows takes five bodies of secular insight seriously, names what each sees clearly, and tests each against Scripture, because every account of why the table works carries a hidden picture of what a person is and what a meal can do, and the picture is where the wisdom is won or lost.

secular.source: The anthropology of ritual and communal meals
secular.author: Mary Douglas and the study of meals as social codes
secular.whatItGetsRight: Douglas and the anthropological study of food showed that meals are never merely about nutrition, that every culture encodes its deepest boundaries, hierarchies, and bonds in who eats what with whom, and that to share a table is to make a statement about belonging. A shared meal draws a line around a community and declares the people inside it kin. This is a precise account of why the early church's open table, where slave ate beside master, was read by everyone as the radical social claim it was.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The anthropology reads the social grammar of the meal correctly and stops at the threshold of what makes the Lord's table unlike every other. Douglas can show that meals encode belonging and cannot account for a meal whose host is the crucified and risen Lord and whose bread, Scripture says, is a participation in his body. The Supper does mark a community, but it does so by joining that community to a person, not merely to one another. The science rightly recovers the table as a code of belonging. The gospel names the One the belonging is to, and he is not a social construct but a living Lord.

secular.source: The psychology of embodied and ritual memory
secular.author: Research on embodied cognition and remembering through the body
secular.whatItGetsRight: A large body of research has shown that human beings remember and are shaped far more deeply by what they do with their bodies than by what they merely think, that repeated physical ritual lodges meaning in a person below the level of conscious thought, and that the things we taste, touch, and enact form us in ways no lecture can. This is a striking confirmation of the wisdom of a Lord who gave his people a truth to eat rather than only a doctrine to recite, knowing they were bodies and not just minds.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The science illuminates how the Supper forms us and cannot supply the One who is doing the forming. Embodied memory explains why a repeated meal shapes a person more than a repeated argument, and Scripture says the bread is not a mere memory aid but a means through which Christ himself is given by his Spirit. A ritual can lodge meaning in the body and still leave the heart unchanged if God does not act. The research rightly recovers the formative power of physical practice. The gospel insists the power is finally not in the practice but in the Christ the practice receives.

secular.source: The sociology of collective effervescence and shared ritual
secular.author: Emile Durkheim and the study of ritual solidarity
secular.whatItGetsRight: Durkheim argued that communities are made and held together by shared rituals, that when people gather to enact a sacred practice together they generate a binding energy and a renewed sense of belonging that holds the group together through ordinary time. His work establishes that a regular, embodied, communal ritual is not decoration but the very thing that turns a crowd of individuals into a people, which is exactly what the New Testament claims the one loaf does.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Durkheim names the binding power of shared ritual and then explains it away, treating the sacred as nothing but the group worshiping itself. Scripture agrees the Supper binds the many into one and insists the binding agent is not the group's own energy but the real body of Christ, who makes them one because they are first joined to him. A church that ate the meal only to feel its own togetherness would be doing what Durkheim described and missing what Paul commanded. The sociology rightly sees that ritual makes a people. The gospel says the people are made one in Christ, not merely in the meal, and the difference is everything.

secular.source: The science of gratitude and thanksgiving
secular.author: Robert Emmons and the research on gratitude
secular.whatItGetsRight: The research on gratitude has shown, with data, that the regular practice of giving thanks measurably reshapes a person toward joy, humility, and connection, and that gratitude is among the most reliable engines of human well-being. The early church's instinct to make thanksgiving, Eucharist, the very name of its central meal turns out to sit on solid ground. A people formed by weekly thanksgiving over bread and cup are being shaped in a direction the science confirms is good for them.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The research confirms that thanksgiving forms us well and cannot tell us whom to thank, and the whom is the whole of the Eucharist. Emmons can demonstrate that gratitude as a practice lifts a life, and a gratitude with no one at the other end is a mood pretending to be a relationship. The Supper grounds its thanksgiving in a specific act of a specific God who gave his Son, so the joy is not a technique run on the self but the natural breath of a creature who has been rescued. The science rightly recovers the power of thanks. The gospel supplies the One whose gift makes the thanks true rather than merely useful.

secular.source: Comfort food and the emotional meaning of eating
secular.author: Research on food, memory, and emotional nourishment
secular.whatItGetsRight: Studies of how food carries emotional and relational meaning have shown that particular foods become bound up with love, security, memory, and belonging, that the meals of our childhood can summon a whole world, and that to be fed by someone is experienced at a deep level as being cared for. This helps explain why a meal, of all the things Jesus could have left, reaches places in a person that propositions never touch, why being fed the body of Christ lands as comfort and not merely as instruction.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The research honors the emotional weight of being fed and reaches the edge of the deepest hunger without naming it. It can show that food carries love and belonging and cannot reach the hunger Augustine named when he said our hearts are restless until they rest in God. The Supper feeds a hunger no earthly comfort food can satisfy, the hunger of a soul for its Maker, and it feeds it with Christ himself. The science rightly recovers that to be fed is to be loved. The gospel names the bread that finally fills, the living bread that came down from heaven, of which a man may eat and never hunger again.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who equally love this meal and equally bow before the Lord who gave it have, for five hundred years, read the words this is my body along different lines, and the difference is not careless. The dividing question is how Christ is present in the Supper, whether the bread and cup are chiefly a means by which the living Christ truly gives himself to the believer, or chiefly a memorial in which a grateful people remember and proclaim a salvation already accomplished. Hear each view at its strongest, because both are trying to honor the same Lord and the same words, and each guards against a real danger it has watched the other risk.

views.view: The Supper as the real giving of Christ to the believer
views.body: This view, held in different forms across the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and much of the Reformed tradition, reads the Supper as a genuine means of grace in which the living Christ truly gives himself to the one who eats in faith. It takes with full seriousness that Jesus said this is my body, that Paul calls the cup a participation in the blood of Christ, and that the church for fifteen centuries was united in believing that something real, not merely remembered, is received at the table. Whether one holds that the elements become the body and blood, or that Christ is present in and with the bread, or that the Spirit lifts the believer to feed on the ascended Christ in heaven, the shared conviction is that the Supper does not merely point to grace but conveys it, that Christ comes to meet his people here and feeds them with himself. Advocates argue that a faith comfortable reducing the Supper to a bare memory has already begun to be embarrassed by the incarnation, that the God who gave himself a body delights to feed his people through bread, and that to drain the meal of real presence is to make the holiest moment in worship a mere act of human remembering. The danger they are guarding against is real, a thinned and rationalist faith that cannot bear mystery, that treats the sacraments as visual aids for ideas the mind could grasp without them, and that ends with a religion lived entirely in the head while the body is fed nothing. Against that, they hold that Christ is the host and the gift at his own table, that the believer who comes with empty hands goes away truly fed, and that the meal is one of the surest places on earth to meet the Lord who promised to be there.

views.view: The Supper as the memorial and proclamation of a grateful people
views.body: This view, held across much of the Baptist, Anabaptist, and broader evangelical tradition and rooted in the teaching of Zwingli, reads the Supper chiefly as a memorial in which the gathered church remembers Christ's death, proclaims it until he comes, and pledges itself afresh to him in faith and gratitude. It takes with full seriousness that Jesus said do this in remembrance of me, that Paul says as often as you eat you proclaim the Lord's death, and that the saving work was finished on the cross, where Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for all time and sat down. The presence of Christ in the Supper, on this view, is the real presence of the Spirit among his gathered people and in the faith of the believer who looks back to the cross and forward to the feast, not a presence located in the bread itself. Advocates argue that the memorial view guards the sufficiency and finality of the cross, that it keeps the church from drifting toward treating the elements as holy in themselves or the meal as a sacrifice repeated, and that it honors the plain force of remembrance and proclamation in Jesus' own words. The danger they are guarding against is real, a creeping superstition that fixes grace into objects, that can leave people trusting a wafer rather than the crucified Christ, and that risks obscuring the once-for-all completeness of Calvary behind a ritual that seems to add to it. Against that, they hold that the table is a holy and serious means of grace precisely as remembrance, that a church which truly remembers the cross and pledges itself to the risen Lord is doing exactly what he asked, and that gratitude looking back to a finished salvation is no small thing but the heartbeat of the meal.

parts.title: What the Table Forms in the One Who Eats
parts.body:
The Supper is not only something you believe about. It is something that does something to you, slowly, over a lifetime of eating it, and the change it works is mostly invisible until you look back and find you have become a different kind of person. The meal that you thought was a five-minute ritual has been quietly forming you all along, in directions you would not have chosen and could not have engineered.

It forms a receiver out of an earner. The deepest reflex of the human heart is to pay our own way, to deserve our standing, to contribute something so that what we are given is not pure gift. And the table dismantles that reflex week after week by giving you nothing to do but receive. You come with empty hands and they are filled. You bring nothing and you are fed the body and blood of Christ given for you. A person who eats this meal in faith for thirty years is being trained, against everything in them, to live by grace rather than by achievement, until the posture of open and empty hands becomes the posture of their whole life before God. That is not a small thing in a world, and a church, that runs on earning.

It forms a member out of an individual. You cannot eat this meal alone, not properly, because it is the meal that makes the many one, and every time you take it you are reminded that you do not come to God as a solitary soul but as part of a body, joined to the people on either side of you whether you like them or not. The table sands away the modern fantasy that faith is a private matter between you and God. It puts a brother on your left and a sister on your right and says you are one loaf now, and it sends you out unable to despise the people you have just eaten beside. Over years it makes you the kind of Christian who instinctively thinks we and not only I, which is exactly the kind the New Testament knows.

It forms a rememberer in a forgetful age. We forget everything, including the cross, including the love that bought us, and we drift within a week back into living as though we were on our own. The table is God's mercy against our forgetting. It hauls us back, again and again, to the one Friday that changed everything, and plants the death and resurrection of Jesus not just in our memory but in our mouths, so that we cannot finally lose the center of the story. A people who eat this meal regularly are a people being kept, against the tide of their own forgetfulness, near the cross.

And it forms a person who lives toward a feast. The meal leans forward into a hunger it cannot yet fill, the marriage supper of the Lamb, the day when the table is finally full and the long ache is healed. To eat the Supper is to be reminded, every time, that you are not home yet, that this is the appetizer and not the banquet, and that the deepest hungers of your life are not meant to be satisfied this side of that day. This does something rare to a person. It frees you from demanding that your marriage or your work or your church be the heaven they were never meant to be, and it lets you receive them instead as good gifts on the way to a better feast. The Christian formed by the table is the most patient and the most hopeful person in the room, fed enough to keep walking and hungry enough to keep longing, eating a small taste of the kingdom that is surely coming.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: The Supper is not a doctrine to settle but a meal to receive, and most of what is wrong with how we eat it can be cured not by a better theory but by a better practice, by coming to the table differently and letting it do its slow work. What follows is a concrete path from your next communion to a life shaped by the table, for ordinary believers who want to recover what they have been holding without knowing it. Begin with the very next time the bread and cup come to you.

steps: Before the next communion, read slowly through the words of institution in one of the Gospels and in First Corinthians eleven, and notice what Jesus actually says and does. Come to the table having heard his voice that week, so that the bread and cup arrive already full of his words and not empty.

When the bread and cup come to you, do the one thing the Supper asks above all, receive. Open your hands. Let the gift be a gift. Resist the urge to manufacture a feeling or finish an inventory of your failures, and simply let yourself be fed by a grace you did not earn and cannot repay.

Make peace with someone before you take it. Paul ties the meal to discerning the body, the church, so look across the room or across your life at the brother or sister you are at odds with, and let the table push you toward the reconciliation it was given to enact. Do not eat the meal of oneness while nursing a division.

Examine yourself rightly, which means honestly and then gratefully. The point of examination is not to decide whether you are good enough, because you are not and the table is for sinners, but to come clear-eyed about your need and then to receive the One who meets it. End in thanksgiving, not in shame.

Learn the four meanings of the meal until they come to mind at the table on their own, the new Passover, the communion with Christ, the oneness of the body, and the foretaste of the feast. Take one each week into your communion and let it deepen what had become a routine, until the bite of bread is thick with meaning again.

Read the history of the Supper honestly and charitably, learning how Augustine, Luther, Calvin, Zwingli, and the Catholic tradition understood the presence of Christ. Come to know why faithful Christians have differed, not so you can win an argument, but so you can hold your own conviction with humility and your brothers with respect.

If your church takes the Supper rarely, sit with the question of why, and if you are able, advocate gently for taking it more often. The early church broke bread weekly and the table was the heartbeat of its life. A meal Jesus told us to keep doing was not meant to be a quarterly event squeezed in around the edges.

Pay attention to how your church practices the table, the sealed cups and the silent isolation, and ask what could make it more clearly the one-loaf meal Paul describes. Even small changes, a common loaf, a moment of greeting, eating it as a body rather than as scattered individuals, can begin to recover what was lost.

Connect the Lord's table to your own table at home, and let the one teach the other. The God who feeds you with bread and cup in worship is the same God who gives you daily bread, so let your family meals and your hospitality to outsiders become small echoes of the grace you receive at communion, tables of welcome opened to the stranger.

Take the Supper as your regular school of grace for a whole season, coming to it deliberately as the one place you do nothing but receive, and watch what it does to the rest of your striving life. Let the empty-handed posture of the table begin to spread into how you pray, how you work, and how you stand before God on your hardest days.

Let the table reconcile you to the church you are tempted to leave or despise. The meal makes you one with these particular people, the irritating and the immature and the ones who voted differently, and to keep eating it with them is to be slowly cured of the consumer faith that treats the church as a service to be graded. Stay at the table and let it make you a member.

Read a serious book on the Supper from a tradition not your own, and let a faithful Christian who sees the meal differently stretch your understanding. You do not have to agree to be enriched, and a believer who has only ever heard their own tradition explain the table has only heard half of what the whole church has confessed about its most precious meal.

Build your life around the rhythm of the table as a fixed point of return, a regular reckoning with the cross and the coming feast that anchors a forgetful soul in the one story that holds. Let the Supper be, year after year, the place you are hauled back to grace when you have drifted, and trust its slow formation more than your own resolve.

Teach the meaning of the Supper to your children and to younger believers, so the meal is not a mystery they endure but a gospel they can taste. Tell them why there is bread and why there is a cup, tell them the story of the Lamb, and let them grow up knowing that the center of the faith is something you eat together until Jesus comes.

Carry the table outward into a hospitality that mirrors it, opening your home and your meals to those who cannot repay you, the lonely and the stranger and the not-yet-believing, so that the grace you receive at the Lord's table overflows into the tables you set. A people fed by grace become a people who feed others, and the watching world reads the gospel in a welcome it cannot explain.

Keep coming to the table for the rest of your life, through the seasons of faith and the seasons of doubt, the years it feels alive and the years it feels like dust, trusting that Christ is faithful at his own meal even when you cannot feel him. Eat it until the day you eat it new with him in the kingdom, at the only table that finally matters, the marriage supper of the Lamb, where the hunger that the Supper kept alive in you will at last be filled, and the meal will have no end.

kicker: The Lord's Supper and the Table of Grace
